subject: pharmacology
title: Routes of administration and drug absorption

steps.tx: Routes of administration decide how fast and how completely a drug reaches the circulation. **Bioavailability** is the fraction of the administered dose that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged. An intravenous dose has a bioavailability of one, because it skips absorption entirely. Oral drugs may fall short for two reasons: incomplete absorption across the gut wall, and **first-pass metabolism** in the intestinal wall and liver.
steps.say: Routes of administration decide how fast and how completely a drug reaches the circulation. Bioavailability is the fraction of the administered dose that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged. An intravenous dose has a bioavailability of one, because it skips absorption entirely. steps.tx: Drugs cross membranes mainly by **passive diffusion**, and only **unionised** drugs that are lipid soluble pass easily. The pH rule decides where a drug is absorbed. Weak acids stay unionised in the acidic stomach, so they are absorbed there. Weak bases stay unionised in the alkaline intestine, so they are absorbed there. Aspirin and phenobarbitone are therefore absorbed from the stomach.

steps.tx: **Ion trapping** occurs when a drug becomes ionised on the far side of a membrane and cannot diffuse back. Aspirin stays unionised in the stomach lumen, then ionises inside the gastric mucosal cell and gets trapped there, which adds to its gastric toxicity. Ion trapping also explains why acidic drugs accumulate in alkaline compartments and basic drugs in acidic ones.

steps.tx: The diagram follows **unionised aspirin** as it leaves the acidic lumen and diffuses through the cell membrane, then splits into charged particles inside the cell. The resulting **ionised aspirin** cannot cross back, so it stays trapped and accumulates, adding **mucosal injury** to the known gastric toxicity. This one way shift, called **ion trapping**, also parks acidic drugs in alkaline spaces and basic drugs in acidic ones.
steps.say: Unionised aspirin diffuses from the acidic stomach lumen through the cell membrane, then ionises inside the mucosal cell. The ionised form cannot diffuse back, so it stays trapped and injures the mucosa. This ion trapping also explains why acidic drugs collect in alkaline spaces and basic drugs in acidic ones.

steps.tx: **Prodrugs** are inactive as given and are converted to active drugs in the body. Enalapril becomes enalaprilat, levodopa becomes dopamine, and becampicillin becomes ampicillin. Captopril and lisinopril are ACE inhibitors that are active as given, so they are not prodrugs. Prodrugs offer better bioavailability, greater stability and fewer side effects.
